We conclude that while this highly magnetised NS engine successfully delays prompt BH formation and may launch low-power precursor jets (with powers up to ${\sim} 10^{46}~{\rm erg/s}$) capable of generating observable X-ray flares, it lacks the energy budget to unbind the massive envelope, potentially setting the stage for a subsequent BH-driven explosion.

title: Excited-State Effects in Nucleon Sigma Terms from a Variational Analysis
abstract: We investigate excited-state effects in nucleon sigma-terms in lattice QCD using twisted-mass clover-improved fermion ensembles. We study correlation functions with nucleon and multihadron nucleon-$\sigma$-meson interpolating operators. The analysis is performed using three gauge ensembles, including one ensemble simulated with two degenerate light, a strange, and a charm quark with quark masses tuned to approximately their physical value. We solve the generalized eigenvalue problem that arises from the matrix of correlators and show that the three-point function for the light sigma-term obtained using the optimal linear combination of interpolating operators has substantially reduced time dependence without loss of statistical precision. We apply Laplace filtering and investigate residual excited-state contributions in the extraction of $\sigma_{\pi N}$. Using the same optimal linear combination of correlators as for $\sigma_{\pi N}$ for the strange sigma-term we also observe suppressed excited state contributions over an extended range of source--sink time separations. For the charm sigma-term, we observe negligible time dependence within the large statistical uncertainties, and these improvements show no significant effect.

title: Universal enhancement of the pairing gap in a dilute Fermi superfluid
abstract: At zero temperature, a dilute Fermi gas with an attractive contact interaction forms a superfluid with gapped fermionic excitations. We show that the gap at weak coupling can be organized as a trans-series expansion in the interaction strength and the asymptotic Gor'kov-Melik-Barkhudarov gap. Low-energy virtual quasiparticles generate corrections that are linear in the gap with a leading coefficient nearly 25$\times$ larger than the other known coefficients. This substantially increases the gap at intermediate densities, highlighting that systematic corrections are crucial for quantitative predictions.

title: Prospects for modelling odd and odd-odd nuclei using energy density functionals
abstract: About half of particle-bound nuclei have an odd number of nucleons. About one quarter more are odd-odd, meaning they have an odd number of neutrons and an odd number of protons. In this context, it is about time to shift the 70-odd-year focus of theories using nuclear energy density functionals (EDFs) away from the remaining one-quarter of even-even nuclei. This White Paper aims to present open, unresolved problems and promising research directions in nuclear EDFs that were discussed during the 2024 ESNT workshop in Saclay, France, on ``The microscopic modelling of odd-mass and odd-odd nuclei''.

title: Binding energies in the $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ fermion--antifermion channels from the ladder Bethe-Salpeter and Schr\"odinger equations
abstract: In this work, we calculate the binding energies of an equal-mass fermion--antifermion system in the $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ channels from the ladder Bethe--Salpeter (BS) equation with scalar, pseudoscalar, and vector exchange. The results are compared with those of the Schr\"odinger equation with the corresponding leading static interaction in two regimes: pointlike massless exchange at weak coupling and finite-mass exchange with monopole form factors at stronger coupling. For the BS calculation, we use two independent numerical methods based on momentum-space integral equations and coordinate-space differential equations. The differential-equation method gives estimated relative binding-energy errors below $10^{-9}$ in both regimes. For massless vector exchange in Coulomb gauge, the numerical results are consistent with the uncrossed-ladder perturbative spectrum through the $O(m\alpha^5)$ terms. The results for massless scalar exchange and vector exchange in Feynman gauge are consistent with the common Wick--Cutkosky expansion through order $m\alpha^3$. For finite exchange masses, the differences from the leading static Schr\"odinger spectra at the same masses, couplings, and form factors depend strongly on the exchange and channel. Scalar exchange gives nearly degenerate channels with much weaker binding than the Schr\"odinger reference. In contrast, vector exchange with only the metric term retained gives stronger binding than the Schr\"odinger reference in $0^{-+}$ and weaker binding in $1^{--}$. Notably, retaining the full Proca numerator substantially increases the vector binding in both channels. Pseudoscalar exchange also supports bound states and favors $1^{--}$, although its leading static central interaction vanishes.

title: Physics with Radioactive Ion Beams at the Nuclear Science Laboratory
abstract: The University of Notre Dame is home to a rich history of nuclear science efforts, including some of the earliest developments in the production and creation of radioactive ion beams (RIBs). The resulting TwinSol facility stands as the longest continuously-operating RIB facility in the United States, and has enabled a wide range of experimental efforts in nuclear structure, astrophysics and fundamental symmetries through in-flight RIBs one to two nucleons from stability. A recent upgrade to TwinSol via a third solenoid constituted the founding of the TriSol facility, which provides cleaner, better-focused RIBs to downstream experiments. In this paper, we present a summary of RIB science at the Nuclear Science Laboratory (NSL) with both TwinSol and TriSol and discuss recent upgrades and future experimental plans at the facilities.

title: MoEDAL-MAPP: the first dedicated search experiment at the LHC
abstract: This special issue brings together a collection of original research articles and review papers addressing topics directly related to the MoEDAL-MAPP experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The experiment is designed to search for (meta-)stable, anomalously ionising particles predicted by theoretical extensions of the Standard Model. Several contributions explore the theoretical and phenomenological aspects of models of particular relevance to the experiment, including scenarios involving magnetic monopoles, highly electrically charged particles, and millicharged particles. Other contributions focus on experimental developments, highlighting novel detection techniques and technological advances aimed at identifying these unconventional signatures and probing new phenomena beyond the Standard Model.

title: Linac Coherent Light Source II injector commissioning and early operational experience
abstract: The Linac Coherent Light Source II (LCLS-II) is designed to generate 4 GeV electron bunches at an up-to-1-MHz-high repetition rate to drive x-ray free electron lasers. It has been in user operation since 2023 and has progressively ramped up the beam repetition rate to 93 kHz to date. The LCLS-II 1-MeV electron source was successfully commissioned between 2018 and 2020. The full-scale LCLS-II injector, operating above 75 MeV, began commissioning in 2022 and transitioned to operations a few months later. The LCLS-II injector has demonstrated the ability to deliver a high-brightness, low-emittance electron beam at high repetition rates, meeting key performance targets. However, several operational challenges have emerged during commissioning and early user operations. These include substantial gun dark current, the dependence of bunch charge generation and free-electron laser pulse intensity on the beam repetition rate, the formation of cathode quantum efficiency craters and bumps, significant emittance growth through the laser heater chicane, beam breakup, and the presence of beam halos. This paper presents recent progress in addressing these challenges, along with injector emittance measurements and optimizations, and the first demonstration of operating a laser heater undulator at the third-harmonic resonance.

title: Fast Monte Carlo calculation of multiple scattering in resonant neutron capture
abstract: A fast Monte Carlo code has been developed to calculate multiple neutron scattering in a sample. Good agreement with an independent Monte Carlo calculation using SAMMY is obtained for neutron capture in $^{197}$Au over the energy range 50--300 eV. For capture following two or more scattering events, a difference is found between the direct Monte Carlo calculation and the analytical approximation in SAMMY. The computational speed allows the scattering correction to be recalculated whenever trial resonance parameters are changed during parameter estimation. The computational core is implemented in C++, while data preparation, calculation control and analysis are performed in Python. Model studies examine how Monte Carlo statistics affect the accuracy with which neutron and radiative resonance widths are recovered.

title: Electron cloud energy distribution measurement and model in the LHC with the Vacuum Pilot Sector
abstract: Electron cloud effects constitute a major performance limitation in high-intensity particle accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). A key ingredient for understanding and modeling these effects is the energy distribution of electrons impinging on the vacuum chamber walls. In this paper, we present direct measurements of electron cloud energy distributions obtained in the LHC Vacuum Pilot Sector (VPS) using retarding field analyzers with a beam pipe diameter of 8 cm, i.e., twice the LHC arc one. The VPS provides a dedicated, fully instrumented test environment for electron cloud studies under real LHC beam conditions. The measured energy spectra systematically exhibit a low-energy component associated with secondary electron emission and a higher-energy component originating from bunch-driven acceleration. To characterize these features, a phenomenological model is developed to reproduce the observed distributions up to 3 keV. Model parameters are extracted from a large dataset of LHC fills, with a representative 2025 physics fill used for detailed illustration. The evolution of the accelerated-electron peak is analyzed throughout the fill cycle and compared with predictions from the analytical kick approximation model. Good agreement is observed—particularly during the stable beam phase in one beamline—confirming that bunch-induced kicks dominate the electron energy gain in the field-free regions, as for the VPS. Discontinuities in the peak energy at operational transitions, as well as the recurrent observation of narrow accelerated peaks in the other beamline, are reported and suggest a dependence of the beam optics on the resulting energy gain. Finally, cumulative energy distribution functions are derived to quantify the fraction of electrons exceeding given energy thresholds. These results establish a quantitative experimental reference for energy-resolved electron cloud modeling in the LHC, providing direct inputs for electron cloud simulation benchmarking, heat load estimates, ESD modeling, and residual electron background assessment in ion diagnostics.

title: Applications of a novel model-based real-time observer for electron density profile control experiments in TCV
abstract: Abstract Real-time estimation and control of the electron plasma density profile is fundamental for monitoring and regulating particle confinement, fusion power, heating efficiency, exhaust performance, impurity concentration, and proximity to the density limit (Greenwald et al Nucl. Fusion 28 2199–207) in present and future tokamaks. This work presents the experimental applications of a multi-rate electron density observer (Pastore Fusion Eng. Des. 192 113615) based on RAPDENS (Blanken Fusion Eng. Des. 126 87–103), integrated into the TCV plasma control system, to control the density profile in a range of plasma scenarios relevant to future fusion power plants. Three main experimental contributions are reported. First, the observer enables control of the line-averaged electron density within the last-closed flux surface ( NEL LCFS ) in ohmic, nitrogen-seeded plasmas with alternative divertor geometries, decoupling upstream density from scrape-off layer pickup in the interferometer signal—a limitation of the traditional control scheme. Second, local control of the central electron density below the ECH cutoff is demonstrated in L-mode plasmas with mixed ECH and neutral beam injection heating, where auxiliary-heating-induced profile peaking is treated as a disturbance to the control task. Real-time estimation and adjustment of the electron pinch velocity-to-diffusivity ratio ν / D improves the spatial accuracy of the profile reconstruction, especially in the core region. The underlying turbulent transport in this scenario is characterised via linear and non-linear gyrokinetic simulations with GENE, confirming quantitatively a TEM-dominated pumpout regime during ECH, which affects the amount of gas flux needed to sustain the target density reference. Last, simultaneous control of the edge-normalised density fraction and toroidal beta is demonstrated in high-performance H-mode plasmas ( β N ≈ 2.15 , f GW ≈ 0.80 ), yielding reproducible scenarios with a device-agnostic density metric and robust handling of interferometer fringe jumps.

title: Unconditional full vector magnetometry using spin selectivity in Nitrogen Vacancy centers in diamond
abstract: Quantum sensors based on nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have been a central topic in the sensing community for more than a decade. The extraordinary properties at room temperature of the spin system in diamond have made it one of the most prominent quantum platforms for the development of commercial quantum sensors. In particular, the sensitivity of the electronic spin in NV centers has made diamond-based magnetic sensors of special interest for their potential application in medical, industrial or navigation solutions. However, the use of these sensors for universal vector magnetometry was constrained by the need for previous knowledge on the field being measured to fully exploit their benefits. In this work, we show a method to perform unconditional vector magnetometry without the need of external information on the magnetic field, based only on the spatial arrangement of the diamond and the microwave antenna combination. While previous NV-based vector magnetometry methods require partial knowledge of the magnetic field (e.g. a calibrated bias field), we exploit the possibilities of selecting particular directions of the spins in the diamond with elliptically polarized microwave fields. We prove that our method allows to estimate both magnitude and direction of external magnetic fields without further assumptions or constraints.

title: Physics at the Edge: Benchmarking Quantisation Techniques and the Edge TPU for Neutrino Interaction Recognition
abstract: This work presents a benchmark of quantisation techniques for convolutional neural networks applied to neutrino interaction recognition, motivated by the need for low-power inference close to the detector in future liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) experiments. Using simulation of a generic LArTPC, four Keras models are trained to classify neutral-current, muon-neutrino charged-current and electron-neutrino charged-current interactions, quantised using post-training integer quantisation and quantisation-aware training, and deployed on the Google Coral Edge TPU. Latency and energy per event are compared with those of an Intel Core i7-13650HX CPU, a consumer NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and a data-centre NVIDIA A100 GPU, using measured energy at different batch sizes and thread counts; the energy of the Edge TPU is estimated from its nominal power. The accuracy degradation is strongly model-dependent: InceptionV3 shows no significant loss along either pipeline, whereas the other models are substantially degraded. At batch size 1, the Edge TPU is comparable to or faster than the CPU and 1.3-6.5 times slower than the A100, while requiring 5--70 times less energy per event than the other devices; with batching, the GPUs reduce this gap to a factor of 2.6-7.2. The Edge TPU is also approximately four times cheaper than the consumer GPU and more than two orders of magnitude cheaper than the A100. Its low power per device eases deployment where power and cooling are constrained, with an additional benefit in terms of environmental impact. This paper explores possible future integrations of edge AI technologies with neutrino physics.

title: Long-Delayed Afterpulse Measurement of JUNO 20-inch Photomultiplier Tubes
abstract: In large-scale liquid scintillator detectors such as the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), high-intensity events like cosmic muons induce photomultiplier tube (PMT) afterpulses that can interfere with the analysis of delayed physics signals. To systematically evaluate this instrumental background, we present a dedicated measurement of long-delayed afterpulses in two types of JUNO 20-inch PMTs: a dynode-based PMT and a microchannel-plate (MCP) PMT. The afterpulse time profiles were first characterized within a direct 1.8~ms waveform window and were further extended to 20~ms using a sliding-window readout strategy. Distinct long-delayed components are observed, revealing a strong dependence on the PMT multiplication structure. The dynode PMT exhibits a broad afterpulse component peaking at approximately 260~$\mu$s, whereas the MCP-PMT shows a pronounced peak around 90~$\mu$s, an additional component around 550~$\mu$s, and a much smaller, broadly distributed millisecond-scale component. For the microsecond-scale components, the afterpulse yield per primary photoelectron is at the $10^{-3}$ level in the selected delayed windows and increases approximately linearly with the primary light intensity. The accumulated delayed activity can therefore become non-negligible following high-intensity events. These quantitative findings provide critical inputs for PMT response characterization and for the accurate modeling of delayed correlated backgrounds in high-precision neutrino experiments.

title: A single radiation hard pixel detector for proton dosimetry, imaging, energy resolution and beam monitoring
abstract: Proton therapy enables highly conformal tumour irradiation by exploiting the Bragg peak. Clinical precision relies on detector systems that provide linearity, spatial resolution, radiation hardness, and, for ultra-high-dose-rate (FLASH) therapy, high dynamic range with sufficient temporal response. No compact all-in-one solution currently fulfils all these requirements. Here, we present pixelated gallium nitride (GaN) arrays as a multifunctional platform. These detectors exhibit high linearity (proton currents from 70 to 1700 pA cm-2) and signal uniformity below 2% across 128 pixels. To probe GaN radiation hardness, we applied cumulative doses up to 6.7 MGy at energies from 25 MeV down to the Bragg-peak regime. Locally deposited dose dictates long-term signal loss, yet devices preserve linearity and spatial response. We demonstrate 0.25 mm effective spatial resolution, validated against radiochromic film. Proton radiography resolves fine tissue structures, with the dose extrapolated to 7 mGy per 1 ms frame in a prospective single-shot configuration. Energy-dependent responses match GATE/Geant4 simulations, and wedge measurements enable Bragg-peak tracking with an energy resolution below 10 keV in an optimised geometry. Real-time ms-scale beam monitoring enables live dose verification.These results establish GaN pixel detectors as a scalable and radiation-hard platform, enabling dosimetry, beam monitoring and energy verification in one device.

title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
abstract: Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction. We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions. Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent with the phase diagram of a type-II superconductor. This links the double pulses to a superconducting material in the SiPM, likely an adhesion layer or diffusion barrier introduced during manufacturing. The mechanism by which the superconducting state produces the second pulse is not yet understood.

title: Warhead Verification with Neutron Beams and Electric Cryptography
abstract: Future arms control treaties may need to reliably verify warheads for dismantlement as part of the treaty verification process without exposing carefully guarded weapons information. Neutron Resonance Transmission Analysis has been proposed as a strategy to verify the authenticity of nuclear warheads and warhead components slated for dismantlement in an arms control verification exercise. Most actinides have resonant neutron absorption lines in the eV region, so by measuring the energy resolved transmission of neutrons and observing the resulting isotope-specific absorption lines, the authenticity of a nuclear device can be verified. To ensure acceptance of this technique by treaty partners, the measurement should minimize information learned about the warhead, including both geometric and isotopic features. Past implementations of transmission analysis acquired and compared neutron time-of-flight spectra. We have developed an analog electric cryptographic measurement proof of concept system where only counts in specific resonance energy windows are observed. The system uses discrete analog components, producing a complete data acquisition and analysis circuit. By limiting the design to easily verifiable parts, the entire apparatus is transparent to authentication and certification. The information security provided by this analog measurement technique may make it the verification basis of future ambitious arms control treaties that explicitly stipulate the dismantlement of nuclear weapons.

title: Scan-Coil Delay Causes Anisotropic Signal Loss in Fast 4D-STEM
abstract: Fast pixelated detectors are driving 4D-STEM toward microsecond dwell times, a regime in which the finite response of the scan deflection coils becomes comparable to the dwell time itself. Using direct probe imaging and sub-frame diffraction analysis, we document a significant intra-dwell scan-coil delay that systematically smears the recorded signal anisotropically along the fast scan direction, with a settling timescale of several tens of microseconds. We present a phase-correlation-based sub-frame alignment procedure that measures and corrects this smearing, and we assess its impact on focused and defocused 4D-STEM reconstructions over a range of scan step sizes. The correction restores signal across a broad range of spatial frequencies, with the largest gains at the large step sizes required for low-dose biological imaging. Because it operates on existing data with no modification to the microscope, the method offers a practical route to recovering signal that would otherwise be lost to scan-coil delay.

title: O-SCOPE: a Raspberry Pi Pico oscilloscope
abstract: In this paper we provide an introduction to some of the efficient features of the Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2) family of microconroller boards (RP2040 and RP2350). More exactly, we show how to use PIO (Programmable Input/Output) and DMA (Direct Memory Access) to program the RP2 boards for efficient DAC (Digital to Analog) and ADC (Analog to Digital) conversions. Using OP-AMPS (Operational Amplifiers) we also show how to build a minimal electronic frontend interface for signal input/output. Finally, we integrate all these components into a product, the O-SCOPE, which is a practical and easy to use oscilloscope and wave function generator. The RP2 component of the O-SCOPE is built using Micropython, while the user interface is developed using vanilla Javascript and it runs on the web browser of any computer, interacting with the RP2 board via the Web Serial API. The O-SCOPE web interface is hosted on GitHub Pages such that it is directly accessible everywhere using a web browser, such that no local installation is required. Also, the RP2 software component is freely distributed on GitHub using the UF2 (USB Flashing Format) mass storage file, and it can be installed by simply dragging the file on the RP2 boards. These features make the O-SCOPE easily accessible, transforming it into a very low cost and useful tool for laboratories everywhere in the world.

title: Interactive event-driven 4D-STEM with Timepix4 and live analytical ptychography
abstract: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy provides access to rich diffraction information at every probe position, but the high data rates associated with pixelated detectors remain a major challenge for interactive operation. Event-driven detectors offer an efficient alternative by representing the measurement as a sparse stream of individual incidences, substantially reducing requirements related to data handling and enabling on-the-fly processing. Here, we develop a high-throughput, real-time, 4D-STEM workflow based on the Timepix4 detector and demonstrate its operation at microsecond dwell times and standard beam currents. A common clock shared by the scan unit and detector allows the probe position of each electron event to be determined directly from its time-of-arrival, eliminating the need for inter-stream synchronization and enabling fully concurrent and independent multi-stream processing. The resulting pipeline continuously processes the detector data during acquisition, with the reconstructed images directly available. We demonstrate live virtual annular detector imaging, Real-Time Integration Center of Mass and direct electron ptychography within the guided progressive reconstructive imaging framework. The workflow sustains the high event rates of Timepix4 while maintaining zero latency for live interactive operation, thus extending event-driven 4D-STEM towards beam currents and acquisition conditions beyond those previously demonstrated with Timepix3-based systems. These results demonstrate that the combination of high-bandwidth event-driven detection, hardware-level synchronization and parallel processing can transform 4D-STEM from an offline technique into an interactive imaging modality, in which dose-efficient phase contrast and diffraction-based signals can serve directly as immediate feedback during STEM experiments.

title: Exploring the proximity effect of thin tungsten-aluminum films for phonon-mediated kinetic inductance detectors
abstract: Lowering the energy threshold of phonon-mediated kinetic inductance detectors is a key step toward next-generation cryogenic calorimeter arrays with large target mass and high sensitivity. In this work, we demonstrate the feasibility of integrating thin tungsten films, so far used for transition-edge sensors, into the fabrication of Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs). Here we present the results from the characterization of a single KID prototype composed of a tungsten-aluminum bilayer of respectively 15 nm and 35 nm thicknesses. The detector was successfully calibrated, and the superconducting film characteristics were measured by operating the device at different temperatures. We show that, by exploiting the proximity effect of superconductors, the device combines the relatively high critical temperature of aluminum with the large kinetic inductance contribution of tungsten. The main feature is a high kinetic inductance, which accounts for 36% of the total inductance, combined with a superconducting critical temperature of around 630 mK.

title: Development of high-resolution timing technique in the past 25 years
abstract: This paper reviews recent progress in high-resolution timing, rate capability, and aging performance of particle detectors in the context of developments over the past 25 years. It focuses on MCP, SiPM, LGAD, 3D silicon, and SiEM detectors and compares their performance with that of gaseous timing detectors. In addition, preliminary results from a simplified simulation program, Mini-TCAD, are presented, indicating that hexagonal 3D silicon cells may provide better drift-time uniformity and timing resolution than square cells.

title: Demonstration of a cryogenic, switchable electron source for low-temperature detector calibration
abstract: We present the realization of a prototype of a compact, switchable electron source operating at cryogenic temperatures, demonstrated at energies ranging from 100 eV to 300 eV, and conceptually extendable to an arbitrary energy range. The electrons are produced via photoelectric emission, induced by a LED illuminating two 400~nm-thick commercial aluminum layers inside a cryostat, and are subsequently accelerated by a voltage of up to 300~V. Detection is carried out with an array of transition-edge sensor (TES) microcalorimeters designed for X-ray detectors, where we successfully observe signals consistent with electrons produced at the source at rates of $\gtrsim$1~Hz and with an efficiency of $\gtrsim 10^{-14}\ e^-/\gamma$. One of the potential applications of this prototype is the development of a calibration method for cryogenic detectors, based on the generation, acceleration, and multiplication of electrons, followed by their conversion into high-energy photons.

title: 1/f frequency-noise reduction in nanomechanical resonators by dissipation dilution
abstract: The frequency noise of a resonant nanomechanical sensor is well understood down to its thermomechanical limit, but the longest useful averaging time is set by a flicker, or $1/f$, frequency-noise floor whose origin has remained unknown. We show that this floor is the thermal noise of the tension. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the tension of a resonator with fixed ends fluctuates by an amount set by the loss angle of its material; for structural damping, these fluctuations produce $1/f$ frequency noise with a flicker coefficient $h_{-1}=E k_{\mathrm{B}} T/(2\pi V\sigma_0^2 Q_{\mathrm{el}})$, with $Q_{\mathrm{el}}$ the intrinsic loss under elongation, that contains no free parameter and is diluted by the tensile stress $\sigma_0$ in the same way as damping is in dissipation dilution. Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $\sigma_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

title: Wormholes in Vegh--dRGT massive gravity: a null-energy transparency theorem, horizon obstruction, and exact isotropic solutions
abstract: Abstract We study static, spherically symmetric wormholes in de Rham--Gabadadze--Tolley massive gravity with the spatially degenerate Vegh reference metric. The effective fluid carried by the massive graviton contributes nothing to the combination of density and radial pressure that the flare-out condition constrains, so it is invisible to the null energy condition along radial light rays. This holds for the whole degenerate class of reference metrics, for all four interaction potentials, and for any static spherically symmetric geometry; the same property singles out the Vegh choice as the only consistent one. The matter alone must therefore violate the null energycondition at every throat, exactly as in general relativity. This corrects a claim repeated across the massive-gravity wormhole literature. We then determine where throats may sit. Wormholes with isotropic pressure fall into two families. One lies beyond the cosmological horizon of the theory's own vacuum and has no static exterior; it is empty in general relativity and is switched on by thegraviton coupling. The other lies inside that horizon and needs a steeply falling redshift. We give exact perfect-fluid solutions for both. In the second family the graviton term can turn the tension at the throat into ordinary pressure. A thin shell closes the configuration, and its surface stresses and its exotic-matter content follow in closed form. The shells are radially unstable, and light rays near the throat trace an unstable circular orbit.

title: Non-Metricity Corrections Approach to Alleviate H0 Tension: The Logarithmic and Nonlinear f(Q) Models
abstract: Abstract The persistent discrepancy between early-time and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant commonly known as the $H_0$ tension remains one of the most pressing open questions in modern cosmology. In this work, we explore whether modifications to the gravitational sector, specifically within the framework of symmetric teleparallel gravity, can offer a viable pathway toward alleviating this tension. We consider two functional forms of f(Q) gravity: a logarithmic model and a nonlinear saturation model, both of which introduce geometric corrections to the standard expansion history without invoking a cosmological constant. Constraining these models through a Bayesian MCMC analysis against a comprehensive suite of observational data, including CC, Type Ia supernovae compilations (Pantheon, Pantheon+SH0ES, and DES SN5YR), and BAO measurements from SDSS and DESI, we find that both models remain statistically competitive with \LambdaCDM. The logarithmic model yields H_0 values that reduce the statistical discrepancy with the SH0ES determination for the considered late-time dataset combinations, with the residual tension quantified using a standard \sigma-based tension metric. Although the AIC, BIC, and DIC information criteria marginally prefer \LambdaCDM over the extended models, the results indicate that the logarithmic model can partially alleviate the H_0 tension for the late-time datasets considered, with the degree of alleviation depending on the specific combination of observations, providing a phenomenological assessment of late-time H_0 tension within the modified gravity framework.

title: Equilibrium-Completion Entropy Potential: A Measure of Thermalization Capacity in Cosmology
abstract: Abstract Entropy production in cosmological nonequilibrium processes can be difficult to characterize when intermediate states lack a well-defined local thermodynamic entropy. Motivated by monopole production and strongly supercooled cosmological phase transitions, we introduce the equilibrium-completion entropy potential (ECEP), a counterfactual measure of equilibrium entropy capacity. For a given underlying theory, the Landau-frame energy density of the actual local state defines a maximum-entropy equilibrium-completion state, whose equilibrium entropy density gives the ECEP. We derive an exact local identity relating the divergence of the associated ECEP current to the mismatch between the actual and equilibrium-completion stresses, and develop corresponding finite-domain balance and resolved-hard matching formulations. As cosmological benchmarks, we show that a strictly equilibrium crossover transition conserves comoving ECEP despite changes in the equation of state and relativistic degrees of freedom, while the equilibrium-completion target of a first-order phase transition generally includes the phase-coexistence branch.

title: Chemical abundances and kinematics of two very metal-poor stars: HE 1421+0022 and HE 2150−1800,
abstract: Abstract We present, for the first time, a detailed high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of two VMP stars, HE 1421+0022 and HE 2150−1800. Both stars exhibit significant carbon enhancement ([C/Fe] ≥+2.0)and enhanced nitrogen abundances ([N/Fe] ~+2.17 and +1.37 respectively). The derived metallicities, [Fe/H] ~−2.79 and −2.48, respectively, place both stars firmly in the VMP regime. We determined the abundances of the light and iron-peak elements C, N, Na, Mg, Ca, Sc, Ti, Cr, Mn, and Ni, as well as the neutron-capture elements Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, and Eu. Based on their locations both stars are classified as Group I objects in the Yoon-Beers diagram of A(C) vs [Fe/H]. Applying established classification criteria for carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars, HE 1421+0022 is identified as a CEMP-r/s star and HE 2150−1800 as a CEMP-s star. Our kinematic analysis shows that HE 1421+0022 is a high-energy, prograde star associated with the outer Galactic halo, while HE 2150−1800 is a high-energy, retrograde star associated with the inner halo. The combined chemodynamical properties suggest that HE 1421+0022 may be associated with either the Sagittarius (Sgr) or Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) accretion event, whereas HE 2150−1800 is likely associated with the I’itoi structure. These results provide further evidence that metal-poor stars in the Galactic halo preserve signatures of accretion events involving dwarf satellite galaxies, offering valuable insights into the hierarchical assembly and chemical evolution of the Galaxy.
source: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: Constraining three-nucleon forces in nuclear lattice effective field theory
abstract: We study short-range three-nucleon forces (3NFs) in nuclear lattice effective field theory with a chiral two-nucleon interaction at N${}^3$LO. The one-pion-exchange ($c_D$) and contact ($c_E$) terms of the leading 3NF are decomposed into locally and non-locally smeared components and supplemented by partial-wave-resolved pair contacts coupled to the density of a third nucleon. We determine their coefficients from nuclear binding energies for nuclei in the mass range from $A=3$ to $A=40$ and neutron--alpha finite-volume energies. This allows to work out the minimal three-nucleon force that can be used for future precision studies in NLEFT.

title: Transport of hard probes in the glasma
abstract: The quark-gluon plasma (QGP) formed in relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC thermalizes from an out-of-equilibrium state of strong classical gluon fields known as the glasma. Jets and heavy quarks, produced in the initial scatterings, traverse these pre-equilibrium fields, but the glasma stage is neglected in phenomenology, which may bias the extracted QGP transport coefficients. This thesis studies its impact on jet and heavy quark transport. The glasma is described in the Color Glass Condensate framework by solving the classical Yang-Mills equations on a real-time lattice. The fields initially form longitudinal electric and magnetic flux tubes whose transverse correlation length is set by the saturation scale $Q_s$. Probes are studied with both classical transport equations and quantum evolution in the light-front Hamiltonian approach. The transport coefficients for jets and heavy quarks are much larger than in the QGP and anisotropic between transverse and longitudinal directions. The azimuthal decorrelation of back-to-back $c\bar{c}$ pairs in the glasma is comparable to that from the QGP, making $D\bar{D}$ angular correlations a potentially measurable glasma signature. The glasma also modifies the nuclear modification factor $R_{AA}$, though the effect is moderate compared to the nuclear parton distribution contribution. A systematic gauge-invariance analysis shows that the distinction between kinetic and canonical momenta is essential when comparing classical and quantum results, and that Coulomb gauge fixing largely reduces gauge artifacts. Finally, the eikonal quantum evolution of a high-energy quark is studied with time-dependent Basis Light-Front Quantization. The resulting momentum broadening agrees with the classical estimates and lays the groundwork for including quantum radiation.

title: Search for Sub-Solar Mass Binaries in the First and Second Part of LIGO's Fourth Observing Run O4a-O4b
abstract: The observation of sub-solar mass neutron stars and black holes would signify a new class of astrophysical objects since these systems are not expected to form via standard stellar evolution. We present the first sub-solar mass search for binaries consisting of neutron star or black holes that uses the data from both the second part (O4b) and first part (O4a) of the fourth observing run of the Advanced LIGO detectors. The search covers primary masses 0.1 to 2 $M_\odot$ and secondary masses 0.1 to 1 $M_\odot$. Tidal effects up to $7\times10^5$ are accounted for in extremely low-mass neutron stars. No statistically significant candidates are identified. We place a $90\%$ confidence upper limit on the merger rate $\mathcal{R}_{90}$ for sub-solar mass black holes and neutron stars to be $< 5.2\times10^{2}\,\textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for a chirp mass of 0.5 $M_\odot$, a factor $2.2 \times$ lower compared to previous O1-O4a searches. We constrain the effective local dark matter fraction to be $\tilde{f}_\textrm{PBH}<0.6\%$ for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}=0.8 \,M_\odot$, approximately $1.5$ factor improvement to previous O1-O4a constraints. Given our model assumptions, our local dark matter fraction constraints are $2-7$ times lower than the OGLE microlensing survey for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}\ge{0.6}~M_\odot$.

title: Progress in Muon Cooling and Moderation Techniques
abstract: Muon beams are essential tools for a wide range of applications such as the search for rare muon decays and muon spectroscopy. However, conventional muon beams produced from pion decay have large emittance and broad momentum spread. Conventional beam-cooling techniques cannot improve the beam quality significantly owing to the 2.2 $\mu$s muon mean lifetime. This has motivated the development of dedicated muon beam cooling and moderation methods. This review surveys the principal approaches, including ionisation cooling for high-brightness muon beams, low-energy muon moderation and frictional cooling for slow muon production, and laser ionisation of thermal muonium for ultra-low-emittance muon sources. The challenges associated with producing slow negative muons and emerging concepts based on cyclotron trapping and muon-catalysed fusion are also discussed. These complementary techniques offer promising pathways towards next-generation muon facilities and precision experiments.

title: Hyperstatistics
abstract: We propose a general approach, named by us hyperstatistics, to treat complex systems, in which Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics breaks down at the domain level of the system. Hyperstatistics preserves the concavity of the nonadditive $q$-entropy. We obtain analytical closed-form expressions for the here proposed ($q, n$)-generalized Boltzmann factor $B_q^{n}$ considering uniform, $\gamma$, Log-normal, F, and the $q$-$\gamma$ probability distribution functions. Remarkably, for all investigated distribution functions, $B_q^{n}$ reduces to a $q$-exponential-type function. To demonstrate the applicability of hyperstatistics, we use a table top experiment of the discharge of a capacitor considering $\gamma$-distributed relaxation times, the pressure decay over time associated with the pumping of $^4$He lines of a closed cycle cryostat, midrapidity data for $\textit{p}$-Pb collisions at the LHC, as well as data set for acceleration distribution in turbulent systems. Furthermore, we deduce the power-law-like $\textit{universal}$ dielectric response using a $q$-generalized $\gamma$-distribution function proposed in this work. Hyperstatistics is applicable to systems with inherent non-Boltzmann-Gibbsian statistics at the domain level. We demonstrate that at the domain level hyperstatistics and superstatistics are equivalent, while at the macroscopic level hyperstatistics recovers superstatistics for $q \to 1$ because the Boltzmann-Gibbs character of the domains is restored, as well as Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics for $n \to \infty$.

title: Rotochemical heating of neutron stars in 2D
abstract: The matter inside a spinning-down neutron star (NS) undergoes a slow compression that may drive it out of chemical equilibrium and, consequently, trigger non-equilibrium nuclear reactions that can heat up the star. This phenomenon is called rotochemical heating, and it is relatively well-investigated in the literature. Historically, it has been studied almost exclusively via 1D spherically symmetric models. However, rapidly rotating NSs are not spherically symmetric. We present pioneering simulations of rotochemical heating in full General Relativity in 2D axially symmetric models without relying on the slow rotation approximation. We explicitly follow thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of rotating NSs as they spin down taking into account both radial and angular distributions of temperature, composition, and mechanical structure. The simplest model is employed: only nucleonic composition, only the non-equilibrium modified Urca process as the main heating/cooling mechanism, and no superfluidity. We analyze the impact of the magnetic field strength as well as the effects of the heat blanketing envelope, initial rotation frequency, NS mass, and core EOS. Most of our conclusions coincide with the results of previous works on this topic, with one important exception. We have found a strong dependence of the cooling curves during the rotochemical heating phases on the core EOS, whereas in the literature it was regarded as very weak. The most likely explanation for this discrepancy is that the authors of the previous works have not considered EOSs with wide enough range of variation of the symmetry energy as a function of density.

title: Pythia-Contrib: a modular contribution framework for the Pythia 8 event generator
abstract: Pythia is a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator used in particle, astroparticle, and nuclear physics, by theorists and experimentalists, to simulate particle collisions. Because of the size and diversity of the user community, it is challenging to address all of the needs for new and varied physics models. This paper describes the Pythia-Contrib system, which allows for third-party developers to contribute code to Pythia without introducing external software dependencies to the Pythia code base.

title: Magnetized black holes with anisotropic matter: degeneracy with the Kerr spin in the ISCO radius and radiative efficiency
abstract: Abstract We study the dynamics of charged test particles around a static black hole surrounded byanisotropic matter and immersed in an external, asymptotically uniform magnetic field. Employingthe Hamilton–Jacobi formalism, we analyze circular orbits, the effective potential structure, innermoststable circular orbits (ISCOs), and radiative efficiency, explicitly accounting for the effects of theanisotropy parameter K, the equation-of-state parameter ω, and the magnetic coupling parameterΩB . Our results show that anisotropic matter primarily modifies the background geometry, generallyshifting the ISCO outward and weakening orbital binding. However, radiation-dominated matter(ω = 1/3) produces smaller ISCO radii than the dust case. In contrast, the external magnetic fieldplays a dominant dynamical role: negative values of ΩB significantly enhance gravitational binding,move the ISCO closer to the horizon, and increase the radiative efficiency to values comparable tothose of rapidly rotating Kerr black holes. By constructing degeneracy maps based on the ISCOradius and radiative efficiency, we demonstrate that non-rotating magnetized black holes surroundedby anisotropic matter can reproduce the ISCO radius and the corresponding ISCO-based radiativeefficiency of spinning Kerr black holes, two quantities that enter X-ray continuum-spectrum fitting.This degeneracy is restricted to these ISCO-based quantities and does not imply an equivalence withthe full phenomenology of the Kerr spacetime.

title: $^{16}$O(p,$\gamma$)$^{17}$F Reaction and the C and O Isotopic Ratios in Red Giant Branch Stars
abstract: The $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O isotopic ratio is a widely used tracer of nucleosynthesis and mixing processes in red giant stars. Its value depends on the rates of the proton-capture reactions responsible for the production and destruction of $^{16}$O and $^{17}$O among which the $^{16}$O(p,$\gamma$)$^{17}$F reaction plays a central role, as it involves both isotopes. This work reports on a new measurement of the $^{16}$O(p,$\gamma$)$^{17}$F cross section carried out at the Laboratory for Underground Nuclear Astrophysics (LUNA) over a center-of-mass energy range of 200 - 380 keV, a region previously unexplored by experimental studies. Two complementary techniques were employed: prompt gamma-ray detection and activation. The results obtained with the two techniques are consistent within experimental uncertainties. From the measured cross sections and existing literature data, we evaluate a new thermonuclear reaction rate, which is then used to demonstrate how simultaneous measurements of stellar carbon and oxygen isotopic ratios constrain the initial mass and the extent of the mixing events in red giant branch stars. In particular, we demonstrate how the $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C abundance ratio is primarily sensitive to the temperature T$_{\textrm{max}}$ attained during mixing, whereas the $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O abundance ratio is highly sensitive to the initial stellar mass M$_i$. Therefore, simultaneous measurements of these isotopic ratios can disentangle and place stringent constraints on M$_i$ and T$_{\textrm{max}}$, and the remaining uncertainty is now dominated by stellar abundance measurements rather than nuclear-physics inputs.

title: Momentum fraction and hard scale dependence of double parton scattering in heavy-ion collisions
abstract: In a previous work, we studied the momentum fraction and hard--scale dependence of double parton scattering (DPS) in proton--proton collisions and the resulting dependence of the effective cross section on the final--state observables. In this paper, we extend those results to heavy--ion ($pA$ and $AA$) collisions, accounting for nuclear effects in the relevant kinematic region, namely shadowing and antishadowing. In addition to modifying the longitudinal parton distributions, these effects also alter the transverse parton distribution of the nucleus, for which we propose a simple new nuclear profile. We further hypothesize that partons inside a bound nucleon are more widely separated than in a free proton. We compute the effective cross section for the available $p$Pb data, obtaining reasonable agreement, and provide predictions for future measurements at the LHC. The observed dependence of our predictions on the final state indicates that DPS in heavy--ion collisions can be used to probe the transverse profile of the free proton and the bound nucleon, primarily in $pA$ collisions, as well as the transverse structure of the nucleus, mainly in $AA$ collisions.

title: Constraints on pion parton distributions at small $x$ from leading-neutron electroproduction data
abstract: We revisit the extraction of parton distribution functions (PDFs) in the pion in a global QCD analysis of pion--nucleus Drell--Yan and leading-neutron (LN) electroproduction data, in view of recent suggestions that uncertainties on the pion PDFs at small parton momentum fraction $x$ are dramatically underestimated. We perform a set of controlled fits that vary the LN data coverage, PDF parametrization, and positivity constraints, determining both the PDFs and pion-nucleon splitting functions simultaneously. While the use of a restricted H1 LN data sample used by the Fant\^omas group is found to enlarge the PDF uncertainties and admit solutions with vanishing gluon PDFs, our global analysis provides a good description of an extended H1 and ZEUS LN database, significantly reducing the parametrization dependence and strongly disfavoring a zero gluon distribution.

title: First ab initio calculations of first-forbidden β transitions relevant for the reactor antineutrino anomaly
abstract: Forbidden β transitions are important for understanding the reactor antineutrino anomaly. Using many-body perturbation theory with two- plus three-nucleon interactions, we have derived the valence-space effective Hamiltonian and effective operators for first-forbidden transitions. 20 dominant first-forbidden transitions have been investigated, which provide important contributions to the reactor antineutrino spectrum anomaly. Calculated log f t values are in reasonable agreement with experimental data. Obtained shape factors exhibit significant deviations from the values approximated with forbidden transitions treated as allowed transitions. The “5 MeV bump” observed in the experimental U 235 -fission antineutrino spectrum was discussed with self-consistent shape factors obtained in the present work. No empirical quenching factors are required in the present calculations of the first-forbidden transitions.

title: Competitive constraints on exotic tensor currents from $EC/\beta^+$ ratios
abstract: We introduce the ratio of electron capture to positron decay rates of unstable nuclei as a probe for exotic tensor currents in the electroweak sector. We calculate nuclear structure corrections and newly derived radiative corrections and obtain competitive limits on exotic tensor couplings using historically available data to find $\varepsilon_T = (1.06 \pm 0.76)\times 10^{-3}$ which is competitive with collider searches and the global $\beta$-decay database. In doing so, we resolve a 50-year-old tension in the strongly hindered $^{22}$Na transition by retaining higher-order operators, obtaining a consistent description of its different weak-decay observables. Finally, we discuss the potential of this method to significantly improve tensor constraints using modern cryogenic quantum sensors.

title: Electron-Ion Collider as a Discovery Tool for Invisible Dark Bosons
abstract: We illustrate how the future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) can be used to discover dark bosons with masses in the $\sim$ (10~MeV -- 10~GeV) regime, having a wide range of properties. We only require that the dark bosons have a non-negligible weak coupling to electrons and decay with $\ord{1}$ branching fraction into invisible final states. Our signal selection takes advantage of the excellent electron beam kinematic measurements and the capability to tag incoherent scattering, as envisioned at the EIC. This makes the EIC a powerful tool for uncovering potential dark sector forces, for a variety of possibilities.

title: The 3He({\alpha},{\gamma})7Be {\gamma}-ray angular distribution: measured, and calculated by effective field theory
abstract: The 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be reaction takes place in several distinct astrophysical scenarios. First, in solar hydrogen burning, 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be controls the competition between the pp-I chain, on the one hand, and the pp-II and -III chains, on the other hand. Its rate directly affects the solar model predictions for the well-measured 7Be and 8B solar neutrino fluxes, which can in principle be used as solar thermometer. Second, in Big Bang nucleosynthesis, 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be is the main production channel for primordial 7Li, the decay product of 7Be. Finally, the reaction is believed to produce radioactive 7Be in astrophysical novae. The cross section of this reaction has been studied previously using different methods, namely 7Be activation, 7Be recoil detection, and in-beam {\gamma}-ray detection. The latter studies have in many cases been performed with just one detector in close geometry. Here, for the first time a comprehensive measurement of the 3He({\alpha},{\gamma})7Be {\gamma}-ray angular distribution is reported. Altogether 22 high-purity germanium detectors were used, arranged at 27-145 degrees angle with respect to the beam direction. Data were taken at 442-1213 keV center-of-mass energy. In addition, one data point for the astrophysical S-factor was obtained with the activation method. The angular data are compared with the predictions from a hybrid theoretical approach, where the E1 transitions are modeled using a cluster-based effective field theory (EFT) while the M1 and E2 transitions within an EFT-inspired framework. Good agreement is found, if the interference among these multipolarities is taken into account in the theory.

title: O 16 ( p , γ ) F 17 Reaction and the C and O Isotopic Ratios in Red Giant Branch Stars
abstract: The O 16 : O 17 isotopic ratio is a widely used tracer of nucleosynthesis and mixing processes in red giant stars. Its value depends on the rates of the proton-capture reactions responsible for the production and destruction of O 16 and O 17 among which the O 16 ( p , γ ) F 17 reaction plays a central role, as it involves both isotopes. This work reports on a new measurement of the O 16 ( p , γ ) F 17 cross section carried out at the Laboratory for Underground Nuclear Astrophysics (LUNA) over a center-of-mass energy range of 200–380 keV, a region previously unexplored by experimental studies. Two complementary techniques were employed: prompt gamma-ray detection and activation. The results obtained with the two techniques are consistent within experimental uncertainties. From the measured cross sections and existing literature data, we evaluate a new thermonuclear reaction rate, which is then used to demonstrate how simultaneous measurements of stellar carbon and oxygen isotopic ratios constrain the initial mass and the extent of the mixing events in red giant branch stars. In particular, we demonstrate how the C 12 : C 13 abundance ratio is primarily sensitive to the temperature T max attained during mixing, whereas the O 16 : O 17 abundance ratio is highly sensitive to the initial stellar mass M i . Therefore, simultaneous measurements of these isotopic ratios can disentangle and place stringent constraints on M i and T max , and the remaining uncertainty is now dominated by stellar abundance measurements rather than nuclear-physics inputs.

title: Laboratory Measurements of Energy Partitioning and Anomalous Electron Heating in Magnetized, Perpendicular Collisionless Shocks
abstract: Abstract We present laboratory results on energy partitioning from supercritical, magnetized collisionless shock experiments ( M A ∼ 8, M ms ∼ 4). We report the first observation of fully developed laboratory shocks that evolve for more than seven upstream ion gyroperiods and have a downstream region that extends for more than four shocked ion gyroperiods. We use Thomson scattering to measure electron and ion temperatures, plasma density, and flow speeds. We directly measure a compression ratio of 3.6 ± 0.3, consistent with shock jump conditions. A foot ahead of the shock exhibits superadiabatic electron and ion heating. The downstream electron temperature exceeds adiabatic and collisional electron–ion heating by ≈30%, implying significant collisionless anomalous electron heating. We find a downstream electron–ion temperature ratio T e ( d ) / T i ( d ) = 0.8 ± 0.3 , consistent with spacecraft observations but outside the range predicted by theory and numerical simulations.

title: Higher-order corrections to beta decays and nuclear structure
abstract: Precision measurements of nuclear $\beta$ decay offer a powerful route to tests of physics beyond the Standard Model, but interpreting measurements spectra and correlation observables requires control of subtle nuclear-structure effects. This chapter develops a framework for calculating higher-order corrections--small contributions that can become important at the precision sought in searches for new interactions. After motivating their role in $\beta$-decay observables (with radiative corrections treated in the accompanying chapter), we introduce the relevant kinematics and multipole expansion of the shape factor, identify the subleading contributions, and present the impulse-approximation multipole operators. We then describe the nuclear many-body methods used to obtain the required states and transition densities, and derive the corresponding operator matrix elements in the harmonic-oscillator basis. Taken together, these ingredients enable systematic calculations of nuclear shape factors beyond the long-wavelength approximation, including higher-order multipoles where needed. By helping distinguish Standard-Model recoil effects from possible signatures of new physics, this framework supports the interpretation of increasingly precise $\beta$-decay experiments.

title: Exact solution of adiabatic time dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov inertia for fission
abstract: An efficient method to exactly compute the adiabatic time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov collective vibrational inertias typical of fission is proposed. The method uses the quasiparticle finite amplitude method to invert the stability matrix of linear response. A comparison with other approaches, such as the exact generator coordinate method inertia and the associated cranking non-perturbative approximation, is conducted. It is found that the behaviour as a function of the collective variable (mass quadrupole moment) is essentially the same in the four cases considered, and substantially differs from the commonly used perturbative approach. It is also found that the magnitudes of the inertias are to a good extent related by single factors that seem to be connected with the effective mass of the energy density functional used.

title: EVALUATION OF PHENOMENOLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE TWO-PROTON DECAY OF THE 45FE NUCLEUS
abstract: Abstract A Green-function formalism describing sequential and virtual two-proton (2p) radi-oactivity is developed on the basis of the multiparticle theory of one-proton decay. In the proposed approach, two-proton emission is treated as two consecutive one-proton transitions connected by the Green's function of the intermediate nucleus, al-lowing both on-shell and off-shell intermediate states to be consistently included. Analytical expressions are derived for the total and partial 2p-decay widths as well as for the angular distribution of the emitted protons.The formalism is applied to the ground-state two-proton decay of 45Fe leading to the ground state of 43Cr within the superfluid nuclear model. Calculations demonstrate a pronounced dependence of the decay characteristics on the choice of the single-particle nuclear potential. It is shown that an appropriate choice of the shell potential allows the experimental decay width and the measured proton angular distribution to be reproduced simultaneously. These results indicate that the proposed Green-function approach provides a consistent description of virtual sequential two-proton decay and offers an alternative framework for the interpretation of true two-proton radioactivity.

title: Silent coverage failures in rare-event searches and a degeneracy index that predicts them
abstract: Searches for new physics in low-background experiments infer a non-negative signal strength from few events and often report an upper limit. Nominal frequentist coverage requires both a valid interval construction and an adequate data model. We study how controlled model departures affect lower- and upper-endpoint coverage for six interval procedures in an exact Poisson counting experiment, dark-matter recoil spectra, and a neutrinoless-double-beta-decay peak search. We introduce the Poisson--Fisher degeneracy index $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PF}}(\delta\nu;\vartheta_0)=(\beta,\gamma)$, which maps a specified expected-count deformation, after projection onto the complete fitted tangent space, to $\beta$, the signed fitted signal shift in profiled standard-error units, and $\gamma$, the Poisson--Fisher norm of the unabsorbed residual. Locally, the sign of $\beta$ identifies the threatened endpoint, while larger $\gamma$ implies greater detectability by the saturated-Poisson goodness-of-fit test used here at a fixed $5\%$ type-I error rate. Across the studied deformations, positive signal-like bias degrades discovery-side coverage while making upper limits conservative; negative signal bias from overestimated signal efficiency can make the upper endpoint undercover. Calibration under the nominal simulator does not protect against misspecification of that simulator relative to the data-generating process. A plausible deformation with large $|\beta|$ and small $\gamma$ may therefore evade diagnosis and should be represented by a nuisance constrained with auxiliary information or included in a defensible envelope. In the exactly collinear constrained-nuisance benchmark, modelling the deformation restores coverage at the evaluated grid points, at a quantifiable cost in interval sensitivity.

title: Observation of top-quark pair production in lead-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}}=5.02$ TeV with the ATLAS detector
abstract: Top-quark pair production is observed in lead-lead (Pb+Pb) collisions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}}=5.02$ TeV at the Large Hadron Collider with the ATLAS detector. The data sample was recorded in 2015 and 2018, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 1.9 nb$^{-1}$. Events with exactly one electron and one muon and at least two jets are selected. Top-quark pair production is measured with an observed (expected) significance of 5.0 (4.1) standard deviations. The measured top-quark pair production cross-section is $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 3.6\;^{+1.0}_{-0.9}\;\mathrm{(stat.)}\;^{+0.8}_{-0.5}\;\mathrm{(syst.)} ~\mathrm{\mu b}$, with a total relative uncertainty of 31%, and is consistent with theoretical predictions using a range of different nuclear parton distribution functions. The observation of this process consolidates the evidence of the existence of all quark flavors in the pre-equilibrium stage of the quark-gluon plasma at very high energy densities, similar to the conditions present in the early universe.

title: Fusion digital twins from imperfect models
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

title: Deconfinement and the Charge Susceptibility Matrix of QCD
abstract: At sufficiently high temperatures, lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) calculations predict that nuclear matter undergoes a rapid crossover to a novel, deconfined state known as the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), in which quark flavors essentially behave like independent particles. Here we explore the nature of this transition by introducing two new thermodynamic observables which we refer to as the diagonality and the rescaled curvature of the QCD equation of state (EoS). By comparing these observables in the case of lattice QCD calculations with those of simple toy models and more sophisticated hadronic resonance models, we show that both the diagonality and the rescaled curvature provide complementary insights into the degree of independence between different quark flavors and the underlying degrees of freedom in the system as functions of temperature. We propose that these observables may help to clarify the nature of the transition region and the onset of deconfinement in nuclear matter.

title: A Low-energy Threshold and Multi-messenger Trigger System for the JUNO Experiment
abstract: Abstract The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) is a 20-kiloton liquid scintillator neutrino detector, located 650 meters (1800 m.w.e.) underground in Jiangmen, Guangdong, China. JUNO is primarily designed for reactor neutrino measurements and has been taking data since 2025. With the largest mass of its kind and an excellent energy resolution, JUNO is a leading observatory for high-precision measurements of MeV neutrinos. The standard global trigger system serves as the primary trigger for JUNO. We present a newly developed multi-messenger trigger system that extends the capabilities of the global trigger by providing a lower energy threshold and an independent monitoring capability. During the 2025 operation, it achieved an effective energy threshold of approximately 110 +/- 10 keV, providing a lower threshold configuration suitable for low-energy event analysis. The system shows the potential to further reduce the threshold to well below 100 keV. Based on the multi-messenger trigger system, an astrophysical monitor has been developed to receive and process external alerts from other messengers, such as gravitational-wave observations. A Transient Neutrino Burst Monitor is integrated to detect short-time-scale neutrino burst events and enables real-time monitoring of transient astrophysical phenomena. The system is sensitive to neutrino bursts from core-collapse supernovae within a distance of about 250 kpc. Content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 licence. Any further distribution of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI. Article funded by SCOAP3 and published under licence by Chinese Physical Society and the Institute of High Energy Physics of the Chinese Academy of Science and the Institute of Modern Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and IOP Publishing Ltd.

title: Probing the 12C+12C fusion reaction via zero-degree spectator measurement in the 12C(14N,αd)20Ne quasi-free reaction
abstract: Abstract The 12 C +12 C fusion reaction is a key physical process in stellar evolution and supernova explosions. It not only determines the late evolutionary fate of massive stars but also directly inﬂuences the critical conditions for triggering Type Ia supernovae in accreting white dwarfs. In this work, the Trojan horse method (THM) was employed to investigate the 12 C(12 C,α0)20 Ne reaction channel of the 12 C+12 C fusion process, using 14 N as the Trojan horse nucleus. Telescope detectors were placed at 0◦ and 15◦ to design two experimental conﬁgurations covering the forward-angle regions where spectator particles are most likely to emerge. By applying the distorted-wave Born approximation(DWBA), two sets of astrophysical S ∗(E) factors for the two-body reaction 12 C(12 C,α0)20 Ne were extracted from the three-body reaction 12 C(14 N,αd)20 Ne and normalized to existing experimental data. The results show that, limited by the overall experimental resolution, the present study cannot resolve ﬁne resonance structures. Within the astrophysical energy region of 0 .5–2 MeV, the extracted S∗(E) factor exhibits an increasing trend toward lower energies. The S ∗(E) factor obtained with the 0◦ conﬁguration shows a ﬂatter trend than that obtained with the 15 ◦ conﬁguration. Supported by the quasi-free reaction simulation results, the divergence between the two data sets may reﬂect a combination of experimental acceptance eﬀects, ﬁnite detector resolution, and possible diﬀerences in the relative contributions of reaction mechanisms. This study provides a systematic examination of the experimental design, quasi-free event selection strategy, and interpretation of the underlying physical mechanisms, serving as a useful reference for understanding the role of the 12 C+12 C fusion reaction in astrophysical processes.

title: Neutron stars with an agnostic dark sector: Core and halo configurations from a two-fluid approach
abstract: The study of dark matter admixed neutron stars has the potential to advance our understanding of dark matter particle candidates. However, the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses restricts a systematic, model-independent study. In this analysis, we employ agnostic hadronic and dark matter equations of state to construct dark-matter-admixed neutron stars within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is characterised solely by its low-density equation of state and mass, and is modelled as a Fermi gas, while hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations. A speed-of-sound parametrisation covers the intermediate density region for hadronic matter and the high-density region for dark matter, so the dark matter equation of state is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency, free from bias toward a softer or stiffer equation of state. Within this agnostic framework, we find that dark matter does not generically compactify the star: light dark matter forms extended halos that raise the tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores that lower it. Consequently, the dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability for light, halo-dominated models to NICER mass--radius data for heavy, core-dominated models. Using current data at $1\sigma$, we constrain the dark matter fraction to $f_{\mathrm{DM}} \lesssim 0.11$ for light dark matter. Being almost independent of any assumed dark-sector microphysics, our framework yields conservative, broadly applicable bounds on the dark-matter content of neutron stars. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in Neutron stars.

versions.title: Neutron stars with an agnostic Dark sector: Core and Halo configurations from a two-fluid approach
versions.abstract: The study of dark matter admixed neutron stars has the potential to advance our understanding of dark matter particle candidates. However, the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses restricts a systematic, model-independent study. In this analysis, we employ agnostic hadronic and dark-matter equations of state to construct dark-matter-admixed neutron stars within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is characterized solely by its low-density equation of state and mass and is modeled as a Fermi gas, while hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations. A speed-of-sound parametrization describes the intermediate- and high-density regimes of both hadronic and dark matter, enabling an agnostic treatment of the dark matter equation of state that is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency and does not favor softer or stiffer behavior. Within this agnostic framework, we find that dark matter does not generically compactify the star: light dark matter forms extended halos that raise the tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores that lower it. Consequently, the dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability for light, halo-dominated models to NICER mass-radius data for heavy, core-dominated models. Using current data at $1\sigma$, we constrain the dark matter fraction to $f_{\mathrm{DM}} \lesssim 0.11$ for light dark matter. By treating the medium- and high-density dark matter equation of state agnostically within a fermionic framework, our approach yields conservative and broadly applicable bounds on the dark matter content of neutron stars. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in neutron stars.
